1. Referring to the code in Lecture 7, write an R script using dbGetQuery() that computes the following for every order in the orders table: 
--> Return one row per order, with 3 extra columns computed by window functions 
a) For each customer, find their latest 'order_id' and 'order_date'
--> The customer's most recent order id and order date
b) The sequential order number for that customer (order_seq: 1st order, 2nd order, etc.,) ordered by 'order_date' ascending
--> Order seq: 1st, 2nd, 3rd order for that customer, with oldest first 
c) The total lifetime count of orders placed by that customer (total_customer_orders)
--> The customer's total number of orders on every row

```{r}
q1 <- dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, "
                 SELECT order_id, customer_id, DATE(order_date) AS order_date, amount, --choosing columns
                 FIRST_VALUE(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id --the first value per customer 
                 ORDER BY DATE(order_date) DESC, order_id DESC) AS latest_order_id, --order by date newest to oldest and for orders in the same date, the largest order id 
                 FIRST_VALUE(DATE(order_date)) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id 
                 ORDER BY DATE(order_date) DESC, order_id DESC) AS latest_order_date, --get the most recent order date 
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id -- orders number for that customer
                 ORDER BY DATE(order_date) ASC, order_id ASC) AS order_seq, --order by oldest first, and when they are both at the same time, order id smallest
                 COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) AS total_customer_orders
                 FROM orders --counts the number of rows per customer id (number of orders per customer )
                 ORDER BY customer_id, order_seq; --this controls how the output is displayed- ordering by customer id and then order_seq per customer 
                 ")
print(q1)
```

2. Referring to the code in Lecture 8:
--> Show that an index makes a query faster, and prove the database actually uses it 
a) Write code to measure elapsed time before creating an index
--> Time the query before any index exists
b) Create an index on orders.customer_id
--> Create an index on orders.customer_id 
c) Use EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to show that the index is used for a query filtering by customer_id
--> Prove an index is used
(before the index it should day SCAN orders meaning it did a full table scan, and after, it should say SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_customer (customer_id = ?))
d) Write code to measure elapsed time before and after index creation
--> Compares elapsed time before vs after

```{r}
#Building the big table 
#80000 orders spread across 5000 customers 
set.seed(42)
n_customers <- 5000
n_orders <- 80000

#randomly assigns a customer to each of the 80,000 orders
cust_ids <- sample.int(n_customers, n_orders, replace = TRUE,
                       prob = rexp(n_customers, rate = 1 / n_customers))
order_dates <- as.Date("2020-01-01") + sample(0:365, n_orders, replace = TRUE) #gives each order a random date in 2020 

#assembles the 5 columns into one data frame 
orders_big <- data.frame(
  order_id    = seq_len(n_orders),
  customer_id = cust_ids,
  order_date  = format(order_dates, "%Y-%m-%d"),
  status      = sample(c("PENDING","SHIPPED","CANCELLED","RETURNED"), n_orders,
                       replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.2, 0.6, 0.1, 0.1)),
  amount      = round(runif(n_orders, 5, 500), 2)
)


#Deletes the old 15 row table and saves the big one into the database under the name orders
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders;")
dbWriteTable(PSTAT132db, "orders", orders_big)

#testing query
dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, "SELECT COUNT(*) AS n_orders FROM orders")  # expect 80000

#Deleting any indexes left over from earlier runs 
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_customer;")
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_cust_date;")
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_cover;")
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_cust_amount;")
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_orders_pending;")

#Query used for every timing and plan
sql_base <- "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 1234;"
n_reps <- 200 #repeat the query so the time is measurable

#a. Measuring elapsed time BEFORE creating an index
print(dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, paste0("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN ", sql_base))) #expecting SCAN 

time_before <- system.time({
  for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) res_before <- dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, sql_base) #sql_base contains SQL you want to examine - reads the rows to select * from orders and look for specified customer id 
})

print(time_before)
avg_before <- time_before[["elapsed"]] / n_reps
avg_before

#b) Creating an index on orders.customer_id 
#stored lookup structure for customer id 
dbExecute(PSTAT132db, "CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);")

#c)EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows the index is used
print(dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, paste0("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN ", sql_base))) #expected SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_customer (customer_id = ?)

#d) measuring elapsed time AFTER creating the index to compare
time_after <- system.time({
  for (i in seq_len(n_reps)) res_after <- dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, sql_base)
})
print(time_after)
avg_after <- time_after[["elapsed"]] / n_reps
avg_after

comparison <- data.frame(
  stage = c("Before index", "After index"), 
  total_elapsed_sec = c(time_before[["elapsed"]], time_after[["elapsed"]]),
  avg_per_query_sec = c(avg_before, avg_after)
)
print(comparison)

#Speed up factor
avg_before / avg_after

nrow(res_before) == nrow(res_after)
```

3. For each order, display the amount of the customer's next order and the number of days until that next order
```{r}
q3 <- dbGetQuery(PSTAT132db, "
                 WITH nxt AS ( --CTE creating a temporary result 
                 SELECT order_id,
                 customer_id, 
                 DATE(order_date) AS order_date,
                 amount,
                 LEAD(amount) OVER( --next order amount only looking at rows from the same customer and order by date 
                 PARTITION BY customer_id
                 ORDER BY DATE(order_date), order_id) AS next_amount,
                 LEAD(DATE(order_date)) OVER ( --same idea, but it fetches the next order's date 
                 PARTITION BY customer_id
                 ORDER BY DATE(order_date), order_id) AS next_order_date
                 FROM orders
                 ) 
                 SELECT order_id,
                 customer_id,
                 order_date,
                 amount,
                 next_amount,
                 CAST(julianday(next_order_date) - julianday(order_date) AS INTEGER) --julianday() converts each date into a plain number, subtracting the 2 gives the number of days between them 
                 AS days_until_next_order
                 FROM nxt
                 ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
                 ") %>% mutate(order_date = as.Date(order_date)) #converts the date column from text into a real R date after the query comes back 

print(q3)
```
